title.en: Juan and His Six Companions: The Golden Egg of King Jaime
title.zh: 胡安與六同伴：海梅王的金蛋

region.en: Balayan, Batangas, Luzon, Philippines (origin of the narrator's tale)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋八打雁省巴蘭彥（故事原鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11b 'Juan and His Six Companions', eBook #8299

summary.en: King Jaime promises his daughter to whoever wins the golden egg from the moss-grown oak on the Mountain of the Golden Egg; fleets of suitors perish. Pedro and Fernando both spurn a begging old man and are killed when their axe-blows on the oak rebound; the pious Juan bathes, dresses, and feeds the old man, who rewards him — the egg, then a golden ship — and six prodigies join him on the voyage: Corrin Corron the runner, Mirin Miron the far-seer, Puntin Punton the sure-shot, Carguin Cargon the mountain-carrier, Soplin Soplon the blower, Oirin Oiron the hear-all. When the thrice-perfidious king still refuses, Carguin Cargon overturns the kingdom, Oirin Oiron overhears the surrender, and Soplin Soplon scatters the pursuing army like chaff; Juan marries Maria and is crowned the same day.
summary.zh: 海梅王允諾：取回苔橡樹上金蛋者可娶公主。艦隊盡沒；佩德羅與費爾南多皆拒施老丐，揮斧時木片反彈斃命。虔誠的胡安為老人沐浴、更衣、進食，得金蛋與金船；六位奇人登船同行——飛毛腿、千里眼、神射手、負山人、吹風者、順風耳。背信三次的國王仍不允婚，負山人傾覆其國，順風耳竊聽降語，吹風者將追兵吹散如草屑；胡安與瑪利亞成婚，當日加冕。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Hilario narrator (hearing it from an old woman of Balayan); archival record. Skilful-Companions cycle in grand style.

passages.text: Not very long after the death of our Saviour on Calvary, a powerful king named Jaime ruled a far-away land, devoted to establishing a strong government of moderation and justice; his daughter Maria was a pearl of the kingdom, and neither Venus nor Helen of Troy could compare with her in beauty. After consulting with his advisers, the monarch proclaimed: 'He who shall succeed in getting the golden egg from the moss-grown oak in yonder mountain shall be my son-in-law and heir.' For five days and five nights crowds of lovers, adventurers, and ruffians set sail for the Mountain of the Golden Egg, but none ever reached the place — some shipwrecked, some driven to strange lands, the rest forced back by horrible sights of broken planks and mangled bodies. Three orphan brothers then rose from obscurity: Pedro, Fernando, and Juan, agreeing that Pedro should try first.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the mountain an old gray-headed man in tattered clothes came limping toward Pedro asking for help, but the selfish Pedro pushed him away with disrespect; when his axe struck the oak, a large piece of wood broke off and hit him in the right temple, killing him instantly. Fernando suffered the same fate as his haughty brother. Juan alone remained: after invoking God's help he set sail, met the same old man, and bathed, dressed, and fed him. 'You shall be amply requited,' said the old man, disappearing; with one stroke of his axe Juan broke the oak in two, and in a circular hole lined with down he found the golden egg. But the shrewd king did not want a rustic son-in-law: 'You shall not marry my daughter unless you bring me a golden ship.' The old man appeared again on the mountain and directed Juan to a splendidly equipped ship that moved smoothly over stumps and stones.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As the golden ship traveled along, Juan gathered six prodigies: Corrin Corron, son of the great runner, who was taking his daily exercise by running around the mountain in less than a minute; Mirin Miron, son of the great Farsight, watching a game seven miles away; Puntin Punton, son of the great Sureshot, about to kill a bat-fly annoying a sheep three miles off; Carguin Cargon, son of the great Strong-Back, carrying a mountain on his shoulders to build a dam — when he cast it down, the whole kingdom was shaken so violently that the inhabitants thought all the volcanoes had burst into eruption; Soplin Soplon, son of the great Blast-Blower, exercising his lungs by blowing down long lines of trees like grain before a hurricane; and Oirin Oiron, son of the great Hear-All, lying with his ear to the ground listening to lovers' ditties twelve miles away.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the palace gate Juan asked for the princess's hand, but the king said, 'Never!' When the ship was beyond the frontier, Juan ordered Carguin Cargon to overturn the king's realm; many houses were destroyed and hundreds crushed. Oirin Oiron heard the king seven miles off promise his daughter if Juan restored the kingdom; the kingdom was rebuilt, but the king again refused, and again the realm was overturned. At last Oirin Oiron heard the tramp of horses and the clash of spears: King Jaime's vast host in hot pursuit, nine miles away. 'Let the army approach,' said Soplin Soplon, and when it was within eight hundred yards he blew forcible blasts that scattered the soldiers and horses in all directions like chaff before a wind; only a handful survived, crippled for life. Again the king sued for peace, and this time kept his word: Juan and Maria were married amidst the most imposing ceremonies, and that very day King Jaime abdicated in favor of his more powerful son-in-law. On the site of the destroyed houses were built larger and more handsome ones — the lumber felled by Soplin Soplon's blasts and carried by Carguin Cargon — and the royal couple and the six gifted men led a glorious life, conquering new lands and ruling their kingdom well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 11 'Juan and His Six Companions'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two boys steal a farmer's cow tied behind his carreton, and the cunning Ambrosio ties himself in the animal's place. When the farmer looks back and shouts, Ambrosio explains that his angry mother once transformed him into a cow, and now, restored, he begs his freedom; the kind-hearted wife of the farmer releases 'by the great mercy of God' the rascal, who rejoins his friend to laugh over the two simple folks.
summary.zh: 二少年偷牽農夫拴在車後的母牛；狡黠的安布羅西奧以自己代替牲口拴在原處。農夫回頭見是個男孩大驚；安布羅西奧哭訴『昔日母親盛怒將我變為牛，今日還形』，農婦心生憐憫，以『上帝大恩』放他自由——頑童與同伴相視大笑。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Manila narrator; archival record. Fansler traces the tale to the Arabian Nights 'Simpleton and the Sharper' and Spanish variants; transformation-by-parental-curse is widespread in serious Philippine etiological myths.

passages.text: There was once a farmer driving home from his farm in his carreton, his cow tied to the back of the cart as he was accustomed to do every evening. Two boys, Felipe and Ambrosio, saw him, and Felipe whispered, 'Do you see the cow tied to the back of that carreton? Well, if you will untie it, I will take it to our house.' Ambrosio approached slowly, untied the cow, handed the rope to Felipe, and tied himself in the place of the animal.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the farmer happened to look back he was frightened to find a boy instead of his cow tied to the carreton, and shouted furiously, 'Rascal, give me my cow!' 'Oh, don't be angry with me!' said Ambrosio. 'Once, when I was a small boy, my mother became very angry with me. She cursed me, and suddenly I was transformed into a cow; and now I am changed back into my own shape. It is not my fault that you bought me: I could not tell you not to do so, for I could not speak at the time. Now, generous farmer, please give me my freedom! for I am very anxious to see my old home again.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The farmer did not know what to do, for he was very sorry to lose his cow; but at home his kind-hearted wife said, 'Husband, what can we do? We ought to set him free. It is by the great mercy of God that he has been restored to his former self.' So the wily boy got off, rejoined his friend, and they had a good laugh over the two simple folks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 15 'The Miraculous Cow'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Clever Husband and Wife: Two Funerals for One Couple
title.zh: 機智夫妻：一對夫妻兩場喪事

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife', eBook #8299

summary.en: Married off with a dowry by his kindly master the doctor, Pedro and his wife Marta squander everything. Pedro reports his own wife dead (onion-juice in his eyes) and receives burial money; Marta reports Pedro dead to the doctor's sister and receives masses money. When doctor and sister compare notes and send servants, the couple take turns lying 'dead' in bed; examined in person, they are found both feigning death — and the delighted benefactor takes them home, laughing at the joke.
summary.zh: 醫師成全僕人婚事並予二百金；夫妻揮霍殆盡後，佩德羅以洋蔥汁拭淚謊報『亡妻』領喪葬費；瑪爾塔又向醫師之妹謊報『亡夫』領彌撒錢。兄妹比對消息互遣僕探，夫妻輪流僵臥裝死；兄妹親至，發現二人在裝死——卻為玩笑與舊僕無恙而大喜，帶他們回家同住。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog droll recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator; archival record. Fansler derives it from the Abu-l-Hasan story of the 1001 Nights (The Sleeper Awakened).

passages.text: Pedro had been living as a servant in a doctor's house for more than nine years and wanted very much to have a wife, but had no business of any kind to support one. His master, noticing his dejection, married him to the woman he loved, let the couple live in a cottage near the hacienda, and gave them two hundred pieces of gold. In time the money was spent, and a second gift of twenty pieces vanished as quickly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Early one day Pedro went to the doctor's house weeping — he had rubbed onion-juice on his eyes — saying that his wife had died and he had nothing for her burial. The doctor pitied him: 'Take this money and see that she gets a decent burial.' A month later Marta went to the doctor's married sister with the same story of her husband's death, and was given money for masses for his soul. That evening the doctor visiting his sick nephew was told that Marta's husband had died — 'No,' answered the doctor, 'it was Marta who died' — and they argued until they decided to send a servant to see which one was dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When Pedro saw the servant coming he told his wife to lie flat and stiff in the bed as if she were dead; the servant reported that it was Marta. The sister would not believe him, so another servant was sent — this time Marta made Pedro lie down stiff and flat, and he was reported dead. Neither knew what to believe, so the next morning the doctor and his sister together visited the cottage and found the couple both lying as if dead. After examining them, however, the doctor realized that they were merely feigning death; he was so pleased by the joke, and so glad to find his old servants alive, that he took them home with him and made them stay at his house.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 16 'The Clever Husband and Wife'; not verbatim.
